clue.text: Reprimand bishop interrupting leading attack

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a side that is leading is up, as in 'two up'
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
a raid is a sudden attack

explanation.surface: A bishop is scolded for barging into an offensive that was already under way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading attack' reads as one phrase, but 'leading' is its own piece: a team that is leading is ahead, as in 'two goals up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are verbs meaning to scold someone severely, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Offer support with constable oddly off

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones, the second, fourth and so on

blocks.note: a prop holds something up
the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the word

explanation.surface: Someone offers to back a policeman whose behaviour has been rather strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' usually keeps the odd letters; 'oddly off' removes them, so the even letters are what survive.
explanation.definitionFit: An offer and a proposal are both nouns for something put forward for another party to accept.

clue.text: Withdraws, having sent up first course, including last of these

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top
the last of a word is simply its final letter
to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the starter is the first course of a meal
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A diner leaves the table after the starter has been served, having eaten the last of them.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'sent up' means the word is read from the bottom, so the meal's opening dish is written backwards before the extra letter goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are present-tense verbs for pulling back or moving away from a position.

clue.text: Doing nothing about father is a crime

indicators.note: about can mean around, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: inaction is the state of doing nothing
Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

explanation.surface: It is suggested that failing to look after one's father ought to be against the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' is not a parent here but the title of a Catholic priest, abbreviated Fr.
explanation.definitionFit: An infraction is a breach of a law or rule, so it can stand for a crime or offence.

clue.text: Person who succeeds in broadcasting tune

indicators.note: broadcasting puts something on the radio, where it is heard rather than read

blocks.note: an air is a melody; the word is pronounced exactly like the one needed

explanation.surface: A performer makes it big by playing a song on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person who succeeds' suggests someone successful, but here succeeding means following on, as a successor does; the H is silent.
explanation.definitionFit: An heir succeeds to a title or property on the death of its holder, following the previous owner.

clue.text: Leisure pursuit for the most part involving no associate

indicators.note: most of something but not all, so the final letter is lost
to involve is to wrap in or include, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a hobby is something done for pleasure in spare time
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes up a pastime that is mostly solitary, with no companion involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Associate' looks like a noun meaning a colleague, but it is the verb meaning to mix with people.
explanation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix socially, especially with people of higher status, which is to associate with them.

clue.text: Leggings good for women in restaurant staff?

indicators.note: for can mean in place of, so one letter is swapped in where another stood

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
W is the abbreviation for women, as on toilet doors
waiters serve the tables in a restaurant

explanation.surface: It asks whether leggings would suit female waiting staff, ending with a question mark.
explanation.walkthrough: The G replaces the W at the front of WAITERS. Gaiters are coverings for the lower leg and ankle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaiters are protective coverings for the lower legs, so they are a kind of legging worn over boots or trousers.

clue.text: Shame men toyed with hidden souvenir

indicators.note: something hidden is concealed inside other material, here the run of letters in the clue

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A tale of embarrassment: some men played about with something and then concealed it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through shaME MEN TOyed.
explanation.definitionFit: A souvenir is a keepsake from a place or event, which is exactly what a memento is too.

clue.text: Set off from assignation outside school

indicators.note: being outside means surrounding, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: a date is an arranged romantic meeting
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: A pupil heads off to a secret rendezvous just beyond the school gates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' suggests leaving for somewhere, but it means triggering an explosion. ETON is the English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb is to make it explode, which is what detonating a charge means.

clue.text: One female in two score, getting brace

indicators.note: one thing placed within another, so these letters go inside a longer word

blocks.note: a score is twenty, so two of them make this number
the Roman numeral for one
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A single woman among forty people ends up wearing a dental brace.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, an old counting word. 'Brace' reads as a noun, as in a pair or a dental brace, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To brace something is to strengthen or reinforce it, and fortify is a verb for making something stronger.

clue.text: Monster keeps clear, seeing this girl

indicators.note: to keep is to hold on to, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: a brute is a savage, monstrous person
to clear a sum as profit is to net it, as on a financial statement

explanation.surface: A monster stays well away once it catches sight of a particular girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' looks like an adjective or 'go away', but it is the accounting verb, as in clearing a profit.
explanation.definitionFit: A brunette is a woman or girl with dark brown hair, so the phrase points to a particular kind of girl.

clue.text: BBC look at different individual offering a shine

indicators.note: making something different changes its form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A viewer urges the BBC to consider a different type of presenter, one with some polish.
explanation.walkthrough: The shine is on shoes, not on screen.
explanation.definitionFit: A bootblack earns a living cleaning and polishing boots and shoes, so is someone who offers a shine.

clue.text: Person, say, with area retail outlet in Spain

blocks.note: bod is informal British slang for a person
e.g. is short for 'for example', which is what say means here
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: Someone opens a shop somewhere in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is a common way of signalling an example, hence EG.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a small Spanish shop, especially a wine shop or grocery, so it is a Spanish retail outlet.

clue.text: Storm club involved with Tudors

indicators.note: something involved is tangled and complicated, so the letters are mixed together

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A club storms into a quarrel with the Tudor royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Storm' looks like a verb about attacking, but it is the noun, a weather event.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloudburst is a sudden, violent downpour of rain, a particular kind of storm.

clue.text: Take out of service cocktail of iced tea attracting tax

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture of ingredients, so the letters are blended into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax

explanation.surface: A bar withdraws its iced-tea cocktail from the menu because it has become liable to tax.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is value added tax, the British equivalent of sales tax; its letters join the iced tea in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To deactivate a machine or system is to switch it off so it stops working, putting it out of use.

clue.text: Crazy rough plan has leader of rebels taken out

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front
something taken out is removed, so a letter disappears

blocks.note: a draft is a first rough version of a plan or document
first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A wild scheme ends with the rebel commander being assassinated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken out' suggests killing the leader, but it only removes the R from DRAFT.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy and daft are both informal adjectives for silly or foolish.

clue.text: New lad is keeping nothing in except something for the windsurfer

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so the letters take a fresh arrangement
to keep is to hold, so one piece is held within another
one thing placed within another, so these letters go inside a word

blocks.note: taken as written
bar means except, as in 'all bar one'
O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A boy is shown staying in and doing nothing, apart from something to do with windsurfing.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled SAILD holds BOAR, itself O inside BAR. 'Except' as bar is a familiar crossword step.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailboard is the board with a mast and sail used in windsurfing, the windsurfer's essential equipment.

clue.text: Part of USA that’s excited but slow to support Democrat

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order
in a down clue, supporting something means sitting beneath it, so one piece follows another

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for Democrat
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lively yet sluggish region of America backs a Democratic candidate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excited but slow' reads as a contradiction; 'but' is part of the letters, not a conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dust Bowl is the region of the American prairies ruined by drought and dust storms in the 1930s.

clue.text: Main line in disarray? It’s flowing

indicators.note: one thing placed within another, so these letters go inside a word

blocks.note: the main is an old poetic word for the open sea
something in disarray is a mess
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A railway main line is in chaos, yet somehow traffic keeps moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main line' reads as railway talk, but main is the sea and the L sits after the M of MESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seamless runs smoothly without breaks or joins, which is what flowing prose or movement does.

clue.text: Offers made by pub workers without impediment

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a part is removed from the longer word

blocks.note: bartenders serve drinks behind a bar
a bar is an obstacle or impediment

explanation.surface: Pub staff make deals without any obstruction.
explanation.walkthrough: BAR is removed from the front of BARTENDERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenders are formal offers or bids, such as a price quoted to do a job, so the plural nouns match.

clue.text: Sells one stocked by roofer given a lift

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting something turns it to read upwards
a shop stocks goods inside it, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: a slater lays slates on roofs
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A shop sells a single item, taken up by a roofer who needs a lift.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'given a lift' means the tradesman is read upwards; the roofer here is one who lays slates.
explanation.definitionFit: To retail is to sell goods to the public in small quantities, so the third-person verbs match.

clue.text: House doctor’s taken advantage of

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A medical man on the house staff has been exploited.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no indicator word; the answer simply lurks in hoUSE Doctor. Dr House is also a TV doctor, a tempting false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: To be used is to be exploited by someone for their own benefit, as the phrase describes.

clue.text: This should keep viewers in touch

definitions.text: This should keep viewers in touch

blocks.clueFragment: This should keep viewers in touch
blocks.note: surface reading: something that keeps a television audience engaged with a programme
setter's reading: the viewers are organs of sight, and touching means meeting another's gaze

explanation.walkthrough: Viewers suggests a TV audience, but they are eyes, and keeping in touch is looking straight at someone.
explanation.definitionFit: When two people hold each other's gaze their eyes stay connected, which is the literal sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Top Gear could be rather passé

blocks.note: first meaning: headwear (top gear) that is worn and elderly
second meaning: out of date and uninteresting

explanation.surface: A viewer grumbles that a long-running TV motoring show has grown stale.
explanation.walkthrough: Top Gear is a BBC motoring programme, but here top gear is simply what goes on top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Something described as old hat is tired and unoriginal, so it is out of fashion or passé.

clue.text: Contents of hints aimed early enough

indicators.note: the contents of a word are its inner letters, with the outer shell discarded

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Suggestions are offered to someone in good time.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word is stripped of its outer letters, and the two insides are joined.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrive in time is to be early enough, not late, for an appointment or deadline.

clue.text: After brown bread, nothing is a lost cause

indicators.note: one thing coming after another means the pieces are placed one following the other

blocks.note: cockney rhyming slang: brown bread rhymes with the word meant
in cricket a duck is a score of zero

explanation.surface: Once the brown loaf is gone there is nothing left, a hopeless situation.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a phrase that rhymes with it; in cricket a batter out without scoring has made a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead duck is an idiom for a plan or person with no chance of success, a hopeless case.

clue.text: Pass trainer’s first young player

indicators.note: the first of a word is just its opening letter

blocks.note: a col is a pass between mountains
opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A coach passes judgment on the leading youngster in the squad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass' looks like a verb about football, but it is a mountain gap. A colt is a young or junior player in a sports team, especially in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: In sport, colts are junior or inexperienced members of a team, so a colt is a young player.

clue.text: Sort of light fitting that’s seen on end of rifle?

definitions.text: that’s seen on end of rifle

blocks.note: first meaning: a bulb fitting with side pins that push and twist into place

blocks.clueFragment: that’s seen on end of rifle
blocks.note: second meaning: a blade fixed to the muzzle of a gun

explanation.walkthrough: The light-bulb fitting takes its name from the push-and-twist way the blade clips onto a rifle.
explanation.definitionFit: The same noun names a push-and-twist bulb mount and the stabbing blade soldiers fix to their guns.

clue.text: Soldiers legally bound to be trustworthy

blocks.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
someone liable is legally responsible

explanation.surface: Soldiers are under a legal duty to be dependable.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Engineers, RE, are a regular crossword source for soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe someone who can be depended on to do what is expected.

clue.text: One on the fiddle from prison is tense

blocks.note: a prison cell
taken as written
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A fraudster sent down from jail is feeling nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the fiddle' is British slang for cheating, but here the fiddle is a stringed instrument; a cello is a big fiddle.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays the cello, a large member of the violin family, which is informally a fiddle.
